To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the neuropeptides PDF and sNPF are produced by different groups of neurons in the Drosophila brain, 2) PDF is produced by a small group of cells that are active at night and sNPF is produced by a larger group of cells that is active during the day, and 3) the PDF and sNFP neurons project to the same target neurons, the large ventral lateral neurons, but they do this at different times of the day,

the neuropeptides PDF and sNPF act as morning and evening signals, respectively, to delay the phase of PER expression in clock cells and that this delay is sufficient to account for morning and evening behavioral activity.

neuropeptides from the two groups of clock cell pairs delay the activity of the morning and evening neurons, respectively, and that these peptides act on their clock cell targets to give rise to morning (CT1) and evening (CT2) behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the circadian clock controls daily behaviors.
the molecular mechanisms underlying circadian clocks and the behavioral outputs of these clocks.
the molecular and cellular mechanisms of circadian clocks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neuropeptides in the Drosophila clock are responsible for the morning and evening activity.
the neuropeptides of the two groups of clock cell neurons act as a molecular clock that regulates the circadian rhythm of the clock cells.
this work demonstrates the existence of a molecular mechanism that is able to control the timing of the activity of circadian clock neurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found that two neuropeptides are responsible for the differential activity of clock neurons at different time points of the day.
the neuropeptides are a key factor in the timing of the clock cells.
neuropeptides from the two groups of clock neurons, the morning cells and the evening cells, delay the activity of their target neurons in a time-of-day dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we identified the first neuropeptide that is required for morning behavior in Drosophia, and the first neuropeptides required for evening behavior.
the neuropeptides are not simply modulating the clock cells but are actually part of the circadian clock itself.
the neuropeptides are likely to be involved in regulating the timing of activity of clock cells, and thus the timing of behavior, in a way that is not understood at present.
